transcript.text: my tumble dryer is giving off a burning smell?? is it safe to keep using it

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Leave it switched off and unplugged until a qualified engineer has checked it. A burning smell from a tumble dryer can be lint overheating in a restricted air path, but it can also be a slipping belt, motor/blower problem, or a heater/thermostat fault. Any of those needs treating as a fire risk. With it unplugged and fully cool, you can safely:
1. Remove and clean the door lint filter. Look for excessive fluff, darkened/scorched areas or a strong burnt smell.
2. Check the lower filter/condenser if your dryer has one, and clear visible fluff from the accessible air path.
3. If it has an external vent hose, check it is not crushed, kinked or blocked. Do not dismantle panels or reach into the machine. Even if you find lint, it should still be inspected before being used again, because the source of overheating needs confirming.
ok I've switched it off at the wall?? the lint filter is really full, I haven't cleaned it in a few weeks. the hose behind is squashed and there's fluff inside the end I can see, is that bad??

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes — that is bad, and it is a very plausible reason for the burning smell. A full lint filter plus a squashed hose containing fluff severely restricts airflow, so heat and lint can build up rather than being carried away. That is a fire-risk pattern. Do not use the dryer again until it has been checked by a qualified engineer, even after clearing the visible blockage. With it switched off, unplugged and fully cool:
1. Clean the lint filter thoroughly. Remove all fluff and check for darkening, melting or a particularly strong burnt smell; those findings strengthen the case for internal overheating.
2. Gently remove only loose fluff you can safely reach at the end of the hose, without pushing it farther in. The hose should then be rerouted so it is not squashed or sharply kinked.
3. If the outside vent outlet is accessible, check it is not visibly blocked by fluff. Do not dismantle the dryer or reach into internal ducting. The restricted filter and hose are likely contributors, but lint may also have collected inside the dryer around hot components, or an overheating protection part may have operated. An engineer should inspect and clean the internal airflow path, fan and heater area before it is put back into service.
